## Simple explanation

Linear algebra is the mathematics of lists of numbers (vectors), rectangular
arrays of numbers (matrices), and operations that transform them. It gives
machine-learning systems a compact way to represent data and compute model
predictions.

## Technical explanation

Vectors and matrices have shapes that determine which operations are valid.
For example, a matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ may represent $n$
examples, each with $d$ features. Multiplying it by a parameter vector
$w \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ produces one score per example:

$$
Xw \in \mathbb{R}^{n}
$$

Dot products, matrix multiplication, norms, and decompositions are common
operations. In neural networks, tensor libraries extend these ideas to
higher-dimensional arrays.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Model inputs, embeddings, weights, gradients, and batches are represented as
arrays. Understanding shapes and transformations helps engineers interpret
model code, diagnose dimension errors, and reason about compute and memory.

## How it works

Each operation has algebraic rules and shape requirements. A dot product
combines corresponding components of vectors; matrix multiplication composes
linear transformations. A model layer often applies a matrix to a batch of
vectors, then may apply a nonlinear activation.

## Practical example

For a batch of 32 examples with 10 numeric features each, the feature matrix
has shape $32 \times 10$. A linear layer with 4 outputs uses a weight matrix
of shape $10 \times 4$, producing output scores with shape $32 \times 4$.

## Common misconceptions

- Array shape is not just bookkeeping; it tells you what an operation means and whether it is valid.
- A matrix operation may be implemented efficiently on GPUs, but large arrays still consume memory and compute.
- Neural networks are not purely linear algebra: nonlinear functions and other operations are essential.
